text:
jamal: quick Q — seeing intermittent hangs and a growing number of TIME_WAIT sockets when streaming Redwood API responses. Using IHttpClientFactory + a Polly WaitAndRetryAsync(3) policy. Pattern is basically:
```csharp
var resp = await client.GetAsync(url, HttpCompletionOption.ResponseHeadersRead, ct);
using var stream = await resp.Content.ReadAsStreamAsync(ct);
using var sr = new StreamReader(stream);
while (!sr.EndOfStream) {
  var line = await sr.ReadLineAsync();
  // process
}
```
Sometimes ReadLineAsync stalls forever and connections pile up. Any pointers on HttpClient lifetime / Polly interaction with streaming?

alex: long story short — retries + unbuffered streaming can blow up. Polly will re-send the request on failure, but the previous response/connection might still be tied up if you didn't drain/close it. A few quick items to check:
- Use IHttpClientFactory (good) and DO NOT create/dispose HttpClient per request. Typed client or factory-managed instance is best.
- Use HttpCompletionOption.ResponseHeadersRead (you're already doing that) and make sure you fully dispose the HttpResponseMessage after the stream finishes.
- Don't apply the retry policy to streaming endpoints — treat them as non-idempotent.

maria: adding config tips — set connection pooling values so leaks are less catastrophic:
```csharp
services.AddHttpClient("redwood")
  .ConfigurePrimaryHttpMessageHandler(() => new SocketsHttpHandler {
    PooledConnectionLifetime = TimeSpan.FromMinutes(5),
    PooledConnectionIdleTimeout = TimeSpan.FromMinutes(2),
    MaxConnectionsPerServer = 100
  })
  .AddPolicyHandler(GetRetryPolicy());
```
Also consider KeepAlivePingPolicy on .NET 6+ if you’re on Linux to avoid stale sockets.

sophie: code-level approach for conditional policies — you can skip the Polly retry for streaming by checking the request or a header. Example using PolicyRegistry / AddPolicyHandler that inspects the request:
```csharp
services.AddPolicyRegistry()
  .Add("default-retry", defaultRetryPolicy);
services.AddHttpClient("redwood")
  .AddPolicyHandler((request) =>
    request.Headers.Contains("X-Stream") ? Policy.NoOpAsync().AsAsyncPolicy<HttpResponseMessage>() : Registry.Get<IAsyncPolicy<HttpResponseMessage>>("default-retry"));
```
Then set `X-Stream: true` on streaming requests. That avoids retries that re-open streams.

ryan: fwiw we had a prod incident where a background consumer retried a streaming GET and duplicated reads plus socket exhaustion. Fix was: 1) no retries for streaming endpoints, 2) ensure we Cancel the token if processing fails, 3) set MaxConnectionsPerServer and PooledConnectionLifetime, 4) when a retry is necessary, buffer small responses only.

jamal: thanks — quick follow-ups: 1) how do you safely cancel + dispose if the consumer code is stuck in ReadLineAsync? 2) any patterns to detect "hung" read vs legitimately slow stream?

alex: for cancellation — pass the same CancellationToken down to ReadAsync/ReadLineAsync and call ct.Cancel(). Also wrap stream read in a linked token with a watchdog timeout:
```csharp
using var cts = CancellationTokenSource.CreateLinkedTokenSource(reqAbortToken);
cts.CancelAfter(TimeSpan.FromMinutes(5)); // per-message watchdog
var line = await sr.ReadLineAsync(cts.Token);
```
Detecting hung reads: track progress timestamps (last-received) and if no bytes for X seconds, consider reconnecting. But be careful — for long-poll/low-frequency streams that will be noisy.

maria: one more: avoid automatic retries at HttpClientHandler level (Expect100Continue timeouts etc). If you need exactly-once semantics for streaming, add an idempotency or resume token at the app layer so reconnections can resume rather than reprocess.

jamal: awesome, I'll try the header approach to disable retry for streaming and add watchdog cancels + pool config.
